title: Bridging Quantum Computing Paradigms toward Semiconductor Yield: A Controlled CV-versus-DV Comparison on Wafer-Map Defect Classification
authors: Yeonhong Kim, Jonghyeok Im, Monu Nath Baitha, Kyoungsik Kim
abstract: Realizing quantum neural networks (QNNs) in industry requires knowing which quantum computing paradigm suits which task. Motivated by AI accelerators and high-bandwidth memory, where die stacking makes wafer-level defect screening central to yield, we study WM-811K wafer-map defect classification (eight classes), comparing the dominant paradigms, continuous-variable (CV) and discrete-variable (DV), under controlled conditions. To isolate the quantum circuit as the sole variable, a shared convolutional backbone (~4.3M parameters) feeds interchangeable heads (classical dense, CV-QNN, or DV-QNN) as the only structural difference; each quantum head is scaled over three sizes (3, 4, 8 qumodes/qubits). The CV head consistently outperforms the DV head: at four qumodes/qubits it reaches 79.7 +/- 1.8% accuracy versus 61.6 +/- 1.4%, a non-overlapping 18-point gap. The advantage is sharpest on the spatially localized Edge-Loc class, easily confused with Scratch, which CV recovers with recall 0.66 +/- 0.06 while DV fails at every size (<=0.05), showing the structured CV layer better captures fine spatial distinctions between defect types. Training curves show the DV limitation is a representational-capacity ceiling, not an optimization failure; at the Fock cutoff used here (d = 2) the CV advantage reflects two intrinsic properties, a structured, neural-network-analogue layer and continuous phase-space encoding, not Hilbert-space dimensionality. On IBM hardware, DV accuracy holds at shallow depth, degrading only at the deepest circuit. Both quantum heads remain below the classical baseline (85.0%), but the controlled setting isolates where a structured head already helps and, as noise and scale improve, which paradigm can deliver practical advantage.
summary: This paper compares Continuous-Variable (CV) and Discrete-Variable (DV) Quantum Neural Networks for classifying defects on semiconductor wafers. By keeping the feature extraction backbone constant, the authors demonstrate that CV-QNNs significantly outperform DV-QNNs, especially when capturing fine spatial details like Edge-Loc defects. The superior performance of CV is attributed to its continuous phase-space encoding and structured layer design.
main_problem: The study aims to determine which quantum computing paradigm, Continuous-Variable (CV) or Discrete-Variable (DV), is superior for classifying wafer-map defects in semiconductor yield assessment.
main_result: The CV head consistently outperforms the DV head, showing a significant advantage (e.g., 79.7% vs 61.6% accuracy at 4 qumodes/qubits) due to its structured design and continuous phase-space encoding.
method: A controlled comparison was performed by attaching interchangeable quantum heads (CV-QNN or DV-QNN) to a shared, fixed convolutional backbone for feature extraction on the WM-811K dataset.
model_or_system: The system is wafer-map defect classification using eight classes. The models compare CV-QNNs (using Gaussian/non-Gaussian gates) against DV-QNNs (using parameterized rotations and CNOT entanglers).
key_observables: Classification accuracy, Edge-Loc class recall (CV: 0.66 vs DV: <=0.05), and performance degradation under varying input noise ($\sigma$).
important_parameters: Circuit size (3, 4, 8 qumodes/qubits), Fock cutoff ($d=2$), and the classical baseline accuracy (85.0%).
main_assumptions: The comparison isolates the quantum head as the sole variable; CV advantage is attributed to structure and continuous encoding rather than just Hilbert-space dimensionality at $d=2$.
figures_summary: Figures compare model architectures, training dynamics (loss/accuracy vs. epoch), and performance robustness against increasing input noise ($\sigma$) for both CV and DV heads.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem context, details the controlled architectural comparison (shared CNN backbone feeding interchangeable quantum heads), presents quantitative results showing CV superiority on specific defect classes, and concludes by attributing this advantage to continuous encoding structure.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, application-driven benchmark comparing two major QML approaches (CV vs DV) in a domain relevant to advanced hardware manufacturing, offering insights into the necessary structural properties for quantum feature extraction.
